definition: A processor or NE that continually unexpectedly sends messages over the fiber network, thus overloading the fiber network with unnecessary traffic.

Faults consisting of arbitrary behavior on the part of failed components, including stopping and restarting execution, sending conflicting information to different destinations, or any behavior attempting to corrupt the system.

An abstracted view of the Network Elements and the fiber optic interconnection network where NE hardware and fiber appear to software as a virtual message passing interface with guarantees about message order and consistency despite malicious faults.
A mode in which software can control and test the operation of network elements. Used by standalone NE test software. One of two power-up modes, but for X38 flight NEs this mode is not used.
A fault containment region configuration with 2 active processors but at least 3 NEs, where the third processor is masked out, possibly powered on to maintain the virtual group.
External signals, errors, or unusual conditions during instruction execution. When they occur, processor state is saved in registers and execution jumps to a predefined exception vector.

A set of hardware with electrical isolation, independent power, independent clocking, and possibly physical separation so that errors inside the region are contained and external errors do not propagate into it.
Any processor exception not mapped to a VxWorks signal.
The process by which network elements achieve synchronization at power up.
A one-way point-to-point connection between the transmitter in one Network Element and the receiver in another.
The process of bringing a processor that is out of synchronization with its virtual group back into sync with the other redundant processors.
Preventing erroneous data from propagating beyond voters by using majority voting or configuring voters to ignore input from a faulty channel.
A reset of the network element triggered when the onboard watchdog timer is not periodically pulsed in time.
A failure declared permanent when all recovery or reconfiguration attempts by FTSS or application-level mechanisms fail.
A reset of an entire channel caused by initially applying power or cycling power.
The time between applying power to the first processor and the fifth processor during system startup.
The process of bringing a lost processor back into synchronization with a redundant virtual group and restoring its internal state such as memory, registers, and timers.
A component of the network element that schedules messages and collectively determines when messages are ready to be sent across redundant NEs.
A non-redundant virtual group consisting of a single processor. In X-38 architecture, each ICP is a simplex virtual group.
A second fault that occurs between the observation of a first fault and the system reconfiguration responding to it.
Any exception mapped to a VxWorks signal.
The period from applying power or asserting reset until the 50 Hz interrupt is enabled, including activities such as IBIT, ISYNC, TNR, processor synchronization, and communication initialization.
The process of coordinating hardware or software entities in time so redundant components operate within acceptable skew.
The mode a network element enters when it cannot synchronize with other NEs and finds itself alone.
Faults such as those caused by single event upsets that can be recovered by FTSS or application recovery mechanisms.
The process of recovering a lost network element and synchronizing it with the working group while aligning its internal state.
A virtual processor composed of processors located in different fault containment regions, capable of accepting work in a parallel processing environment.
A reset applied to the VMEbus.
A reset applied to an NE when processors in other channels agree and trigger a voted reset to recover a faulty channel.
A software-commanded function where synchronized NEs search for and synchronize with a lost NE.

A low-level processor reset that marks the earliest point of system startup, prior to any software execution. Triggers the System Initialization sequence; the boot phase is measured from this event to the enabling of the 50 Hz timer interrupt.

An Instrument Control Processor hosted in the Network Element Fifth Unit (NEFU). Unlike the ICPs on the four main Flight Critical Channels, the NEFU ICP does not have an associated FCP processor loaded, and its presence or absence does not affect the FTSS software load.

A signal sent by an ICP to the FCP virtual group indicating that the ICP has completed its initialization and is ready for operation. The FCP waits up to 2.5 seconds after sending the FCP Ready Sync before expecting this signal; absence of the signal causes FTSS to defer failure detection until the normal ICP presence test.

Hardware boards installed in an ICP that provide digital input/output interfaces to external systems. These boards are typically initialized by the application during the window in which the FCP is waiting for the ICP Ready signal.

The set of three synchronized FCP processors that remain operational after the loss of one FCP processor is detected. The surviving triplex attempts to re-synchronize the failed processor and, if unsuccessful within 2.5 seconds, issues a voted VMEbus reset through the NE to that processor.

A system operating state entered when a fault is detected during Normal Operation. In this state the system is reconfigured to isolate the fault; if a single permanent fault has occurred, the system will be capable of tolerating one additional fault upon return to Normal Operation.

A system operating state entered after System Initialization is complete, in which the FCP has been configured as a fault-tolerant computer and the 50 Hz timer interrupt is enabled. The system meets all performance and functional requirements in the no-fault case; faults detected in this state cause a transition to the Fault Recovery state.

The periodic hardware interrupt generated by the 50 Hz timer that invokes the scheduler to initiate application task execution. Its enablement marks the end of System Initialization and the transition to Normal Operation.

Read-only memory containing the initial boot code executed at hardware reset. After completing IBIT, it calls the manufacturer-supplied VxWorks BSP initialization software, followed by the FTSS System Initialization software.
A dedicated software routine to set up application-level operations
Independent units of execution managed by the operating system to perform specific processing threads
Software structure --- identified by an IP address, port number, and protocol --- used by the application as an endpoint to establish network or inter-process communication links

An operational state that determines which set of rate groups — and therefore which tasks — are active at a given time. Up to five vehicle modes may be defined in the system, each associated with up to three rate groups (50 Hz, 10 Hz, and 1 Hz). A vehicle mode change is requested via an explicit API call from the application; mode changes occur only while the system is in the Normal Operation state.
Configured memory spacing to guarantee that software data structures conform to hardware-required memory boundary alignments.
A startup synchronization signal sent by an FCP to announce its readiness and initiate a timed wait for the ICP's acknowledgment signal.
Essential control functions. These include attitude control, flight control law execution and actuator command loops
A hardware timer within the Network Element that must be regularly pulsed by software to prevent an automatic reset of the Network Element.

Structured data packets. Each message consists of a header (message ID, source NE, timestamp, sequence number, priority), a payload containing one or more of the following: sensor readings, system health indicators, resource utilization metrics, alarm and event data, or configuration state snapshots, and a footer (integrity check and end-of-message marker).
10 ms time slot used to sequence scheduled tasks and complete fault isolation responses
